strengths: The paper addresses a practical and well-motivated problem: improving video detailed captioning without human annotations or stronger teacher models, which distinguishes it from prior pipelines that rely on GPT-4V/Qwen-72B distillation or human preference data.

The agentic closed loop (caption generation → principle-guided scoring → prompt refinement → self-reflection on regressions) is clearly described with formal notation (Eqs. 1–4), and the idea of converting caption–score trajectories into preference pairs with score gaps as a difficulty signal is a sensible and reusable data-construction mechanism.

Experimental evidence is reasonably thorough: comparison against a broad set of 7B general and caption-specialized MLLMs on the VDC benchmark, plus multiple ablations covering the agent components (Tab. 2), training objective (Tab. 3), robustness to principle wording across three independent contributors (Tab. 4), and the iteration count T (Tab. 5), as well as qualitative comparisons (Fig. 3).

The core claim is supported at matched conditions: VDC-Agent-7B improves over the same base model (Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct) by +5.13 accuracy / +0.27 score at similar inference cost (15.5s vs 15.5s), which is a fair, budget-controlled comparison rather than only chasing absolute SOTA.

The ablation comparing test-time self-reflection (Baseline+P+R: 47.10, 164.9s) against the distilled single-forward model (49.08, 15.5s) convincingly demonstrates the practical value of internalizing the reflective refinement during training-time data generation.
weaknesses: Circular self-scoring is the main unresolved concern: preference labels are produced by the same 7B model that generates the captions, and the paper provides no validation that these self-scores correlate with human judgment or with the VDCscore metric (which is itself a learned metric from AuroraCap). Since the scoring principles and the VDCscore evaluation criteria may overlap, the DPO signal may partially optimize toward the model's own notion of quality, and possible length/detail bias (longer captions scoring higher) is not analyzed or controlled for.

Methodological novelty is modest: the agentic loop is a natural combination of ReAct/Reflexion-style reflection with prompt optimization, and 'Curriculum DPO' reduces to sorting pairs by score gap in descending order under a standard DPO loss (Eq. 6 is just vanilla DPO with a fixed batch order). The claimed connection between large ∆s and 'low-variance gradients' is asserted intuitively but never measured (e.g., no gradient-norm or convergence curves supporting the easy-to-hard narrative).

The claim that self-reflection capability is 'internalized into the MLLM' is overstated: the model is only fine-tuned with DPO on best/worst captions from the trajectories; it is never trained to produce scores, suggestions, or reflections, and no experiment shows the trained model can reflect or self-assess better than the base model.

Evaluation is confined to the single VDC benchmark (1,027 videos) with a single LLM-based metric; no general video captioning metrics, no downstream-task evaluation (e.g., video QA or text-to-video retrieval despite these being cited as motivating applications), and no statistical significance or variance estimates for the reported gains (e.g., +0.27 average score over AVC-DPO is within plausible noise).

The absolute improvement over the strongest external-model-free competitors is moderate, and gains on the 'short' dimension are small (+1.73/+0.08), suggesting the approach primarily amplifies detail-centric output rather than broadly improving captioning; the paper's explanation for the short-dimension gap is qualitative only.

No statement about releasing code, prompts (the exact initial prompt p0 and principle text R are not shown), or the VDC-Agent-19K dataset, which weakens reproducibility given that the method is centrally about an automatic data-generation pipeline; minor writing issues (e.g., 'an preference dataset', 'Why self-reflection effective?') remain.

strengths: The paper is clearly written and the pipeline (agentic caption generation -> principle-guided self-scoring -> prompt refinement with a reflection path on score regression -> preference-pair construction -> curriculum DPO) is described end-to-end with enough implementation detail (T=4, lambda=90, LoRA rank/alpha, LR schedule, batch size, hardware) to be reasonably reproducible.

The experimental work is more thorough than typical: ablations cover self-reflection vs. principles at test time (Tab. 2), SFT vs. vanilla DPO vs. curriculum DPO (Tab. 3), robustness to three independently written principle sets (Tab. 4), and the iteration budget T with a compute-quality trade-off (Tab. 5). The T ablation and the test-time-reflection comparison are genuinely informative.

The core claim is supported: a +5.13 accuracy / +0.27 score gain over the same backbone (Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct) at equal inference cost, with the strongest ablation baselines (Baseline+P, Baseline+P+R) reaching only 46.47 and 47.10, and a large T ablation showing the gain is not obtained by trivially iterating at test time.

The motivation is practical: fully automatic preference data construction without human annotations or proprietary/72B teachers addresses a real cost and reproducibility bottleneck in video detailed captioning.
Qualitative analysis (Fig. 3) is consistent with the quantitative claims, and the paper honestly reports where it is not top-ranked (short dimension) and the diminishing returns of larger T.
weaknesses: The central methodological weakness is circular self-evaluation: the same 7B model generates, scores, and refines its own captions, and the final evaluation metric (VDCscore) is itself an MLLM-based judge. Preference pairs are therefore defined by the model's own noisy, potentially self-biased scores, and the pipeline may partly optimize toward what the model already believes is good rather than true caption quality. The paper provides no validation of the scorer's reliability (e.g., correlation of the self-scores with human judgments or with VDCscore), and no human evaluation of the final captions. For a paper whose headline claim is that self-supervision suffices, this is a significant evidentiary gap.

Algorithmic novelty is limited. The 'agentic' loop is essentially iterative prompt optimization with a threshold and a retry path, closely related to existing self-refine/Reflexion-style methods and prior automatic prompt-engineering work, applied here to captioning; the 'curriculum DPO' is simply sorting preference pairs by score gap before training, which is a small variation on curriculum learning with ranked preferences ([31] is cited but the delta from it is not clearly established). The contribution is a well-executed combination rather than a new technique.

Evidence is confined to a single benchmark (VDC) and a single backbone (Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct). There is no evaluation on other captioning benchmarks, no downstream task evaluation (the introduction motivates VDC by VQA/retrieval/text-to-video but none is tested), and no second base model to show the recipe generalizes. For an 'Algorithms/General' contribution claiming a new self-evolving framework, this breadth is thin.

The margin over the most relevant competitor is modest and the comparison configuration is favorable: AVC-DPO-7B reaches 47.70/2.47 and the test-time-adapted baseline (Baseline+P+R) reaches 47.10/2.38 versus 49.08/2.50. No statistical significance, variance over seeds, or confidence intervals are reported anywhere, so it is hard to judge whether the ~1-2 point differences are meaningful.

Table 2 contains an unexplained anomaly: Baseline+P+R scores lower than Baseline+P on the camera dimension (45.15 vs 47.76) despite reflection being an additive refinement, and the text does not discuss it. Relatedly, the DPO hyperparameter beta and the reference policy implementation are not specified.

The 'no human annotations' claim is overstated: the principles R that drive scoring and refinement are human-authored (Tab. 4 even requires three human contributors), and the five task dimensions are taken from the VDC taxonomy. The method shifts but does not remove human design input; the paper should state this more carefully.

The 19K dataset is small relative to competing captioning datasets, and while the per-video generation cost is reported (393.6h on one A800 for T=4), there is no analysis of how performance scales with data volume, only with iteration count T.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated contribution: the paper frames the captioner itself as an autonomous agent that generates, scores, and refines its own captions, removing the two main dependencies of prior VDC work (human annotations and larger teacher MLLMs). This is a practically meaningful and timely direction, appropriate to an Algorithms/General contribution.

The full pipeline is coherent and well described: principle-guided scoring, prompt refinement, regression-triggered self-reflection reusing previous chain-of-thought, trajectory-to-preference conversion, and curriculum DPO exploiting the score gap Δs as a difficulty signal.

Empirical results are convincing for the claimed setting: new state-of-the-art on the VDC benchmark (49.08 Acc / 2.50 score), surpassing caption-focused systems that use human labels or 72B teachers (e.g., AVC-DPO-7B 47.70/2.47, OwlCap-7B 46.90/2.40), with consistent gains over the same-backbone baseline (+5.13/+0.27) at equal inference cost.

Ablations are unusually thorough: (i) decoupling principle injection vs. test-time reflection vs. trained agent (Tab. 2), showing the trained model internalizes reflection without test-time cost; (ii) SFT vs. vanilla DPO vs. curriculum DPO (Tab. 3); (iii) robustness to independently written principle sets by three contributors (Tab. 4); (iv) iteration-budget trade-off (Tab. 5); plus a qualitative comparison with hallucination/error annotation.

Training data construction and filtering are fully automatic and rule-based (20,040 raw sets → 18,886 pairs), supporting scalability and reproducibility; implementation details (LoRA config, LR schedule, hardware, data budget) are reported in enough depth to reproduce.
weaknesses: Self-scoring circularity: caption quality scores and textual suggestions are produced by the same 7B model being improved. The paper never validates that these self-assigned scores correlate with human judgment, so the preference pairs (and the Δs difficulty signal used by curriculum DPO) rest on an unverified proxy. The robustness ablation (Tab. 4) varies principle wording but not this fundamental concern.

Ambiguity about the evaluation protocol weakens the headline comparison: it is unclear whether VDC-Agent-7B is evaluated with the principles text in the prompt. Since Baseline+P alone reaches 46.47/2.35, part of the reported +5.13 gain may come from principle injection rather than the learned internalization; this needs explicit clarification.

Evidence is confined to a single benchmark (VDC, 1,027 videos) with VDCscore — itself a model-based metric (AuroraCap scorer). There is no evaluation on other captioning benchmarks, no human evaluation of the generated captions, and no downstream-task validation (e.g., video QA or retrieval), so generalization claims beyond VDC are unsupported.

Novelty is incremental: the loop closely resembles existing self-refine/Reflexion-style prompt optimization, and curriculum-over-preferences has prior work ([31] is cited). The curriculum component yields only ~1 point over vanilla DPO (49.08 vs. 48.03 average), a small margin without statistical significance or seed variance reported.

The ablation variant 'Baseline+P+R' performs reflective refinement directly on the test set, which is effectively test-time adaptation on the evaluation data; framing this as a comparable variant is methodologically questionable even though the proposed method does not use test data.

Despite the 'no external resources' framing, the method is compute-hungry: T=4 requires ~393.6 GPU-hours of data generation on a single A800, which undercuts claims of cheap self-improvement; the compute–quality trade-off is reported but the cost framing in the abstract/intro is somewhat overstated.

Only one backbone (Qwen2.5-VL-7B) and one dataset scale are studied; scalability of the agentic loop to larger or different backbones is deferred to future work. Minor polish issues remain (e.g., 'an preference dataset', 'Why self-reflection effective?'), indicating the manuscript would benefit from another editing pass.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem framing: the paper targets a real limitation of current VDC pipelines (dependence on human annotations or stronger teacher models) and proposes a fully autonomous generate-evaluate-reflect loop that uses only the base MLLM itself.

The internalization idea is sensible and practically valuable: rather than deploying an expensive test-time agent, the framework distills the agent's trajectories into preference pairs (VDC-Agent-19K) and trains via DPO, retaining base-model inference latency (15.5s vs. 164.9s for test-time reflection) while exceeding its accuracy.

Strong and consistent empirical results: SOTA on VDC and DREAM-1K among ~7B captioners, and consistent gains across three different base models (LLaVA-OneVision, InternVL2.5, Qwen2.5-VL), which supports method-agnostic transferability rather than backbone-specific tuning.

Unusually thorough ablation studies: comparisons against principle injection, test-time reflection, Best-of-N under aligned compute, curriculum vs. random vs. anti-curriculum DPO, sensitivity to maximum iterations T, and robustness to four independently written principle sets (including an industrial guideline set). These materially strengthen the evidence.
Human evaluation with three blind evaluators plus an AI judge with position-bias checks, and a length-distribution analysis to probe the common length-bias confound in preference optimization.

The paper is clearly written, with a clean formalization of the agent loop (Eqs. 1-3), transparent dataset statistics (filtering counts, raw-to-final pair numbers), and full implementation details enabling reproducibility.
weaknesses: Circularity risk in self-scoring: the same model generates and evaluates the captions, so the preference pairs and the curriculum signal (score gap Δs) inherit the model's own biases. The paper validates pairs via human preference (~68-76% preference for y+) and GPT-5.1, but human agreement is not overwhelming and no calibration analysis of the 0-100 scores (e.g., correlation between absolute scores and human judgments) is provided; the score gap is used as a 'difficulty' signal without evidence that it is monotonic with true difficulty.

Limited technical novelty: iterative self-refinement (Self-Refine, Reflexion), self-generated preference data (Self-Instruct, Self-Rewarding LMs, RLAIF-V), and curriculum DPO (Pattnaik et al.) all exist; the contribution is primarily a well-engineered combination plus sorting pairs by Δs. The claimed novelty of 'Curriculum DPO' is modest, and the gain over Random DPO (~1.05 accuracy) is comparatively small, warranting seed-level variance reporting that is absent.

Potential residual length/style bias: mean length differs by ~15% (1106 vs. 1277 tokens) between chosen and rejected captions, and the overlap argument in Fig. 3 is qualitative; no controlled analysis (e.g., preference as a function of length-matched pairs) is provided to fully rule out length-driven preferences that DPO could amplify into verbose outputs at inference.

Sensitivity to the score threshold λ (set to 90/100) is not ablated, despite λ governing both agent termination and the rule-based data filtering; interactions between λ, T, and dataset composition are unexplored.

Training data scale and coverage are limited: 18,886 pairs derived from only 4,008 videos of Cockatiel-4K (a curated, high-quality OpenVid subset), raising questions about diversity and long-video capability; no evaluation on videos with substantially different characteristics (e.g., multi-shot, long-form) beyond the two benchmarks.

Some evaluation details are under-specified or potentially favorable: the VDCscore is itself an LLM-based metric, so gains could partially track judge-model stylistic preferences; the human study reports no inter-annotator agreement, and the 'Project Page' is empty, with several key materials (principles, prompts, pseudo-code) deferred to a non-included appendix, limiting verifiability at review time.

The compute-normalized BoN comparison (Tab. 8) is somewhat unfair to BoN, which uses the same greedy decoding; a sampling-temperature-tuned BoN or self-consistency baseline would make the 'directed vs. undirected compute' claim more convincing.

strengths: The paper presents a complete, self-contained pipeline (agentic self-reflection → preference data construction → curriculum DPO) that is consistently described and easy to follow, and the claimed 'no human annotation, no stronger teacher' property is a practically meaningful goal for video detailed captioning.

Experiments are relatively thorough for this type of work: three distinct base backbones (LLaVA-OneVision-7B, InternVL2.5-8B, Qwen2.5-VL-7B) all improve substantially, which supports method-level (rather than checkpoint-level) claims.

The ablation suite is above average: test-time reflection vs. internalization (Tab. 4, including inference-time measurements), curriculum vs. anti-curriculum vs. random DPO (Tab. 5), robustness across four independently authored principle sets including an industrial one (Tab. 6), iteration depth T (Tab. 7), and a compute-normalized Best-of-N comparison (Tab. 8) that partially rules out trivial test-time scaling as the source of gains.

The human preference study (500 pairs, 3 blind evaluators, position-bias-controlled AI judge) and the length-distribution analysis (Fig. 3) address the two most obvious confounds (self-preference and verbosity bias) at least to a first approximation.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty. The framework is a composition of well-established components: Self-Refine/Reflexion-style iterative self-critique, prompt optimization (PromptAgent), self-generated preference data (Self-Rewarding LMs), and curriculum DPO (Pattnaik et al. 2024, which the authors themselves cite as prior 'easy-to-hard ranked preference' work). The main new element is sorting DPO pairs by self-assigned score gap — a one-line heuristic applied to a new domain. Relative to AVC-DPO, the key difference is replacing an external 72B scorer with the model's own scores, which is closer to a resource substitution than a conceptual advance.

Circular self-evaluation undermines the central claim. Both the preference labels and the difficulty signal (Δs) come from the same Qwen2.5-VL instance acting as judge. The only external verification is 500 pairs rated by 3 humans, with y+ preferred only 67.6–75.8% (17–25% ties). No inter-annotator agreement is reported. A model optimizing toward its own biased scorer could learn stylistic artifacts rather than genuine caption quality; the 500-pair check is too small to fully dispel this concern given the strength of the SOTA claim.

The curriculum result may not be statistically robust. The gap between Curriculum DPO (49.08) and Random DPO (48.03) on a 1,027-video benchmark is ~1 point, with no variance estimates, seeds, or significance tests reported anywhere. Given that the curriculum ordering is the paper's headline algorithmic contribution, this evidence is thin.

Suspicious hyperparameter and design details weaken confidence: λ=90 on a 0–100 self-score is extremely high and unexamined; the best/worst pair is drawn from different task dimensions (e.g., 'short' vs. 'detailed'), so preference pairs may partially encode task-conditioning rather than caption quality; and the 'Short' dimension shows near-zero gain (+1.73), suggesting the gains are partly prompt-level rather than perception-level.

Reproducibility is not adequately supported: the Project Page field is empty, the principles, system prompts, pseudo-code, and dataset details are all deferred to an unavailable Appendix, and no code or data release is stated. Key equations (Eqs. 3, 5) and figures also contain garbled symbols, indicating a rushed presentation.

The efficiency framing is somewhat overstated. While the internalized model matches baseline inference time, data generation consumed ~49–72 GPU-hours on 8×A800, and the comparison to teacher-distillation methods does not account for that generation cost, which weakens the 'eliminates external supervision' narrative as a compute story rather than an annotation story.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem framing: removing dependence on human annotation and stronger teacher models for Video Detailed Captioning (VDC) is a meaningful goal, and the closed-loop generate–evaluate–reflect design is described precisely (Eqs. 1–4).

Comprehensive empirical evidence: results on two benchmarks (VDC, DREAM-1K) across three different base MLLMs (LLaVA-OneVision, InternVL2.5, Qwen2.5-VL) show consistent gains, supporting the method-agnostic claim rather than a single favorable configuration.

Thoughtful and unusually thorough ablations: test-time reflection vs. internalization (Tab. 4), curriculum ordering including an anti-curriculum control (Tab. 5), robustness to four independently written principle sets including an industrial one (Tab. 6), iteration-depth sweep with compute costs (Tab. 7), and a compute-normalized Best-of-N comparison (Tab. 8) that convincingly rules out a pure test-time-scaling explanation.

Good practices for validity checks: a 3-evaluator blind human preference study (Tab. 3), position-bias testing of the AI judge, and a length-distribution analysis (Fig. 3) that preempts the common 'longer captions win' critique.
The paper is well organized and clearly written, with the pipeline, dataset statistics, and filtering rules (20,040 raw sets → 18,886 pairs) reported in sufficient detail to assess data quality.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: the agentic self-reflection loop is essentially Self-Refine/Reflexion-style iterative prompting with a same-model critic, and Curriculum DPO reduces to sorting training pairs by score gap, an idea already present in curriculum-learning and ranked-preference work [5, 51] that the authors cite. The contribution is a competent application/combination rather than a new algorithmic idea.

Potential circularity in the supervision signal is not fully addressed: the same backbone both scores captions and generates them, and the VDCscore judge may share stylistic biases with self-refined outputs. The principle-robustness ablation (Tab. 6) partially mitigates this, but an evaluation with a fully independent judge family, or a cross-model scorer experiment (e.g., scores from a different MLLM), is missing.

Key ablation margins are small and lack statistical treatment: in Tab. 5, Curriculum DPO (49.08) beats Random DPO (48.03) by ~1 point with no variance, seeds, or significance testing; several per-dimension gains (e.g., Short, +1.73) are within plausible noise. The central curriculum claim rests on thin quantitative differences.

The self-improvement loop is validated only against the model's own scores: Tab. 3 shows humans prefer y+ over y− in ~68–76% of cases, which is good but also implies ~24–32% of pairs are ties or reversals — i.e., a non-trivial fraction of the DPO supervision may be noisy, and there is no analysis of how score gap ∆s correlates with human-perceived preference strength.

Reproducibility and release details are incomplete: the project page is blank, there is no statement about releasing code or the VDC-Agent-19K dataset, and several critical components (principles, prompts, pseudo-code, self-reflection trigger rate) are deferred to an Appendix that is not provided, hindering independent verification.

Cost framing could be more candid: although the method avoids external teacher models, dataset construction requires ~49.2h on 8×A800 (Tab. 7) plus multi-round inference; a comparison of total compute against a simple teacher-distillation baseline at equal compute would strengthen the 'resource dilemma' argument.

Minor presentation issues: the claim in Tab. 4 that Baseline+P 'fails to generalize to unseen videos' is confusing (it is a prompt-level method, not a trained adaptation), and some table captions summarize conclusions rather than describing the data, which reads as advocacy and should be tempered.
